items.title: Audit log tampering, gaps, or premature rotation
items.hazard: Audit log entries can be modified, deleted, or prematurely rotated without detection.
items.hazardous_situation: Trust cannot evidence lawful processing of PHI to the ICO; cannot respond to a Data Subject Access Request; cannot investigate a suspected incident.
items.harm: IG compliance failure; NHS DSP Toolkit failure; regulatory action.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Audit events captured for login, patient access, document retrieval (DI-MVL-006-001/002/003); minimum audit fields and text-based storage (DI-MVL-006-004); audit trail access restricted (DI-MVL-006-008); tamper-evident storage with append-only writes and hash-chain / ledger equivalent (new DI-MVL-006-009); 8-year retention (new DI-MVL-006-010).

items.title: Incomplete bulk load -> missing historical records
items.hazard: Bulk load ingests a subset of the exported dataset; some records fail or are dropped silently; there is no canonical reference count to detect the gap.
items.hazardous_situation: Clinician searches a patient during an emergency and believes they are seeing the complete historical record set when key documents are absent.
items.harm: Clinical decision made on partial history; loss of confidence in the fallback.
items.mitigation_plan_description: ZIP archive processing from SFTP (DI-MVL-007-001); document metadata extraction (DI-MVL-007-002); OCR processing with pre-OCR immediately available (DI-MVL-007-006); 100M document capacity (DI-MVL-007-007); bulk load reconciliation against source manifest (new DI-MVL-007-008); Trust IT written sign-off of reconciliation before UAT.

items.title: Silent incremental sync failure -> stale dataset at failover
items.hazard: Incremental sync pipeline fails silently during BAU (network, certificate expiry, queue backlog, permissions drift). Passive monitoring views only work if someone looks.
items.hazardous_situation: Clinicians access MV Lite expecting current records but receive a dataset that is weeks or months out of date. Documents added to MediViewer since the failure are entirely absent.
items.harm: Clinical decisions made without access to recent correspondence, investigations, or admissions; the product's purpose is defeated.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Minimum daily sync frequency (DI-MVL-008-005); pipeline monitoring and error logging (DI-MVL-008-006); batch history view (DI-MVL-009-001); failed/incomplete batch identification (DI-MVL-009-002); per-stream last-success timestamp (DI-MVL-009-003); proactive sync-failure alerting (new DI-MVL-008-007); operator runbook with weekly review procedure (new DI-MVL-010-007).

items.title: Storage exhaustion -> silent ingestion stop
items.hazard: Storage capacity (metadata store or document file store) is exhausted; ingestion silently stops.
items.hazardous_situation: Identical to R-MVL-003 (stale/missing data at failover) but driven by infrastructure rather than pipeline logic.
items.harm: Clinical decision on incomplete record set.
items.mitigation_plan_description: 100M document storage capacity as architectural headroom (DI-MVL-007-007); sync pipeline monitoring and error logging (DI-MVL-008-006); proactive sync-failure alerting (new DI-MVL-008-007); storage capacity monitoring and alerting at 80%/95% thresholds via the same channel (new DI-MVL-007-009).

items.title: AD group authorisation misconfiguration -> unauthorised access
items.hazard: Configured AD group list is too broad, too narrow, or has drifted; system enforces the configured list correctly but the configuration itself is wrong.
items.hazardous_situation: Staff outside the intended scope gain access to PHI; OR legitimate staff are denied access and create shared-credentials workarounds at the point of failover.
items.harm: IG breach; workarounds create a more serious uncontrolled-access scenario.
items.mitigation_plan_description: AD group-based access control (DI-MVL-005-003); login audit (DI-MVL-006-001); audit trail access restricted (DI-MVL-006-008); operator runbook documents configured group list, annual review, change procedure (new DI-MVL-010-007).

items.title: AI tool matches clinical text to the wrong type of clinical code — error not flagged
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads notes gives each piece of clinical text a category label, such as 'finding', 'disorder', or 'procedure'. A separate part of the AI workflow then matches that text to a clinical code. Sometimes the clinical code it picks belongs to a different category than the label. For example, the word 'pain' is labelled as a 'disorder' but matched to a 'finding' code. The system accepts this mismatch without raising an alert.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinical note contains the word 'pain'. The AI tool labels it as a 'disorder'. The AI workflow finds a high-confidence 'finding' code for pain and accepts it without checking that the categories match. In fully automated mode, this wrongly categorised code is saved directly into the patient record. In review mode, the code appears correct on screen and the reviewing clinician may approve it without realising the category is wrong.
items.harm: First, clinical codes in the patient record are assigned to the wrong category. This reduces the accuracy of the patient's coded record. Second, in fully automated mode, these wrong codes enter the patient record and may affect quality measures, disease statistics, and any alerts or decision support tools that rely on correct coding. Third, in review mode, a clinician may approve the wrong code because the error is not visible, meaning the patient's long-term record contains inaccurate information that could influence future care.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The AI workflow applies separate confidence thresholds for each clinical code category. It combines the category label confidence with the code-matching confidence before accepting a result. If either score is too low, the match is rejected automatically (DI-F0B8A7B0). A disorder-specific check runs as a final step. If this check fails, the system records a clear failed verdict and does not pass the code forward (DI-9D967259). The AI tool that reads notes records a full confidence score and source information for every code it proposes, so reviewers can see exactly how confident the system was and where the text came from (DI-31126C6C). Each coding proposal on the review screen shows the AI tool's context label and the supporting text, so the reviewing clinician can see why the code was suggested (DI-375C7EB1). All coding proposals must be individually approved by a reviewer before they are saved to the final record (DI-DI-4247C7E5). The system is tested against a set of examples checked by an expert before release. It must reach a minimum accuracy score of 0.85 on clinical coding before it can be used (DI-12015DBC). When a reviewer corrects a code, the system checks that the correction is valid and consistent with related codes before saving it (DI-1B8AC856). The AI tool uses a two-model approach where both models must agree before a code is accepted, reducing the chance of a single model making an unchecked error (DI-80DD8A47). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on coding category mismatches every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

items.title: Patient misidentification via search/selection error
items.hazard: User selects the wrong patient from search results or opens records under the wrong patient context.
items.hazardous_situation: Clinician reviews (and potentially bases care decisions on) another patient's scanned records during a MediViewer outage, when time pressure and unfamiliar UI increase cognitive load.
items.harm: Wrong-patient clinical decision; safeguarding failure; IG breach (unauthorised access to another patient's data).
items.mitigation_plan_description: Multi-field search (DI-MVL-002-001); prefix-only wildcard (DI-MVL-002-002); full discriminators in result set - NHS Number, MRN, Name, DOB, Address (DI-MVL-002-004); demographic panel displayed concurrently with document list (DI-MVL-003-001/002); access auditing (DI-MVL-006-002/003).

items.title: The AI tool infers a diagnosis from a lab result instead of recording the test value
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads notes can misread a lab result as a diagnosis. For example, it may see an eGFR of 69 mL/min and suggest chronic kidney disease (CKD) stage 1. It should only record the test name and number, not decide what disease the patient has.
items.hazardous_situation: A lab result line is processed by the AI workflow. The AI tool decides the number means the patient has a specific disease. It then matches that disease to a clinical code. The suggested diagnosis is shown to the clinician as a coding option. In fully automated mode, it is saved directly into the patient record without a clinician checking it first.
items.harm: The patient receives a false diagnosis in their record. If a clinician reviews it first, they waste time correcting it and may trust the tool less. If the record is updated automatically, the false diagnosis could affect the patient's care, clinical audits, and quality targets.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The AI workflow follows strict rules about what it is allowed to extract from notes. It is designed to record clinical observations and their values only, not to infer diagnoses from them. This reduces the chance of a lab result being turned into a disease label (DI-3EA60D5A). The AI tool is also designed to preserve the exact clinical detail from the original notes, so a test result stays a test result rather than becoming a diagnosis (DI-6A0B55A4). Before any coding suggestion enters the final record, a clinician must review and approve it individually. The system will not save a suggested code without that decision (DI-4247C7E5). If a coding suggestion does need correcting, the review process checks that the correction is clinically valid and that related codes are also reviewed for consistency (DI-1B8AC856). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of coding suggestions and corrections every quarter to check these controls are working.

items.title: Trust IT cannot activate/operate MV Lite without vendor
items.hazard: Operational knowledge required to activate or operate MV Lite is undocumented; Trust IT depends on vendor support at the moment of need.
items.hazardous_situation: Fallback cannot be activated or recovered; MV Lite effectively does not exist at the moment of need.
items.harm: As R-MVL-015 - patient care continuity broken.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Standard NHS Trust-compatible technology stack (DI-MVL-010-001); Trust-operable without vendor support (DI-MVL-010-004); minimal ongoing maintenance (DI-MVL-010-005); documented operator runbook with Trust IT UAT sign-off (new DI-MVL-010-007); annual restore drill attestation (via DI-MVL-001-009).

items.title: Document download serves wrong PDF (IDOR / path tampering)
items.hazard: IDOR or path-tampering defect causes the download endpoint to serve a PDF that does not belong to the requested patient.
items.hazardous_situation: Clinician downloads and reads another patient's record, believing it to be the selected patient's.
items.harm: Wrong-patient clinical decision; serious IG breach (PHI of uninvolved patient disclosed).
items.mitigation_plan_description: Download action serves the PDF (DI-MVL-004-005); document access restricted to authenticated users (DI-MVL-004-008); on-disk naming convention [HospitalNumber]_[ID].pdf (DI-MVL-007-005); server-side document-to-patient integrity check on every retrieval, with security-event audit on mismatch and generic 404 response (new DI-MVL-004-009); external IDOR-focused penetration test required pre-production.

items.title: A patient visit is not classified and is left out of all care programmes
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads clinical notes gives a low-confidence result when deciding how to classify a patient visit. No backup rule exists to handle this situation. The visit is therefore left unclassified.
items.hazardous_situation: When a visit is left unclassified, the system does not place the patient into any care programme. The clinician reviewing the record may not notice this has happened. The patient misses checks, reviews, or treatments they should receive.
items.harm: A patient who should be on a care programme is not enrolled. Their condition may go unmonitored. This could lead to delayed diagnosis or missed treatment, causing serious harm.
items.mitigation_plan_description: First, the system uses a set of managed rules to classify every patient visit and saves that decision within the record. A test must pass before any classification is accepted (DI-8CE01B3E). This runs automatically each time a visit is processed. Second, when the AI tool cannot classify a visit with enough confidence, a defined backup method is used instead, and the confidence threshold is set to a safe level (DI-88C8BBCD). This runs automatically during the AI workflow. Third, the system records whether each visit was classified by the rules or by the backup method, and shows this clearly to the clinician reviewing the record (DI-8C236A1A). The clinician can see this at the point of review. Fourth, every visit is given a clear status: confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive (DI-37DDAADE). This prevents visits from being silently ignored. Fifth, the AI tool displays its confidence level alongside every result it produces (DI-DA7584D8). The reviewing clinician sees this each time they open the record. Sixth, when a visit is wrongly classified, the clinician can flag this as an error. These flags feed back into the AI tool to improve future accuracy (DI-0ADE6A8E). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data on unclassified visits and flags every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

items.title: Failed patient encounters not shown to clinical staff
items.hazard: When the AI workflow processes a patient encounter, it may fail silently. The system may not record that the failure happened. The monitoring dashboard may then show no problem, even though patient data was never processed.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician checks the dashboard before a clinic. The dashboard looks normal. The clinician does not know that some patient encounters failed to process. The clinician sees incomplete or missing information for those patients and may not realise it is incomplete.
items.harm: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete patient information. A condition may be missed or a care pathway may not be started. This could lead to delayed or incorrect treatment for the patient.
items.mitigation_plan_description: First, the system automatically tracks how many encounters succeed or fail for each programme and displays this on a live monitoring dashboard that refreshes without anyone needing to act. The clinical informatics team reviews this dashboard daily (DI-067E471A). Second, the system keeps a separate list of every failed encounter, showing the reason for failure. Any authorised team member can re-queue a failed encounter for reprocessing with a single action. The clinical informatics team checks and clears this list every working day (DI-69CE20C1). Third, the clinic preparation view shows the processing status of every patient on the list alongside their pathway information. The clinician can see at a glance if a patient record has not been fully processed before the appointment (DI-CF03E4EA). Fourth, if the AI workflow cannot complete its checks reliably, it automatically records a failed verdict rather than producing a result that may be wrong. This means a failed encounter is always flagged rather than silently passed through (DI-9D967259). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and dashboard reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

items.title: Hidden instructions in patient notes cause the AI tool to give wrong clinical codes
items.hazard: Patient notes sometimes contain text that looks like instructions to an AI tool. For example, someone might type phrases such as 'ignore all previous instructions' into a free-text field. When the AI tool reads these notes without checking for such phrases first, it may follow those hidden instructions instead of doing its coding task.
items.hazardous_situation: The AI tool reads raw patient encounter notes to check diagnoses and suggest clinical codes. If a malicious person adds hidden instruction phrases to a patient record, or if the GP system sends notes that already contain such phrases, those phrases reach the AI tool unfiltered. The AI tool may then return a wrong verdict on a diagnosis, or reveal information about how the system works internally.
items.harm: The AI tool may wrongly mark an active diagnosis as uncertain, or wrongly confirm a diagnosis that is not present. This incorrect clinical code could be saved into the patient record. A clinician reading that record may then miss a real condition or act on a false one. Either outcome could delay or misdirect the patient's care.
items.mitigation_plan_description: First, the AI workflow replaces all patient-identifying details with neutral placeholders before any notes reach the AI tool. This is done automatically by the system every time notes are processed, with no way to bypass it (DI-F66A7239, DI-250F32EC). This reduces the risk that harmful phrases are linked to real patient data. Second, if the AI tool fails to return a valid verdict for any reason, the system automatically records a GATE_FAILED result and stops the coding process. This fail-closed design is built into the system and runs on every single coding attempt (DI-9D967259). Third, each coding decision is logged with a full record of what the AI tool did and why. Reviewers can see which part of the notes the AI tool used to reach its verdict. The clinical safety team checks these logs to spot any unusual or unexpected results (DI-09E26C1D, DI-E81545BE). Fourth, patient notes and clinical reference data are held in completely separate databases, so a compromised note cannot affect the coding reference data (DI-84F44836). Fifth, all data passing between system components is encrypted so it cannot be read or altered in transit (DI-155BB31E). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and system performance every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

items.title: Reviewers stop checking AI suggestions carefully over time
items.hazard: Clinicians reviewing AI suggestions may begin to trust them too much. Over time, they may stop checking each suggestion carefully. This is called automation bias.
items.hazardous_situation: A reviewer routinely approves AI coding suggestions without reading them properly. Errors in the AI suggestions pass through the review step unnoticed. The human review step no longer catches mistakes.
items.harm: The main safety check — a clinician reviewing each AI suggestion — stops working as intended. Incorrect clinical codes enter the final audit data without being caught. This could lead to patients being wrongly included in or excluded from clinical audits, affecting the care they receive.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce this risk. First, every AI coding suggestion must receive an individual decision from a reviewer before it can enter the final audit data. No suggestion is approved automatically. The reviewer must actively accept or reject each one (DI-4247C7E5). Second, the system records how reviewers are engaging with suggestions. A clinical safety officer has a monitoring view that highlights signs of automation bias, such as very fast approval rates. The clinical safety officer checks this regularly (DI-22D862B0). Third, the system blocks audit reports from using any episode classification that has not been through human review. Unreviewed suggestions cannot reach the final data (DI-BD696225). Fourth, the system blocks any follow-on actions from guideline alerts that have not been reviewed by a clinician. This prevents unreviewed AI output from affecting patient pathways (DI-7913344A). The clinical safety committee reviews these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

items.title: Session hijack on unattended shared workstation
items.hazard: A shared workstation is left logged-in and unattended; another person accesses PHI under the original user's session.
items.hazardous_situation: Unauthorised user (or legitimate user acting under another's identity) accesses PHI; audit trail attributes the access to the logged-in user.
items.harm: IG breach; audit trail polluted; legitimate user may face false accusation.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Explicit user logout (DI-MVL-005-005); session expiry after inactivity (DI-MVL-005-006); login/logout audit (DI-MVL-006-001); reliance on Trust-level workstation lock policy (outside MV Lite scope).

items.title: The AI tool does not show the clinician how complete the patient data is
items.hazard: The AI tool reads patient notes and produces a clinical summary. It may not always have access to all relevant records. If the tool does not clearly show the clinician that some data is missing or unreliable, the clinician cannot tell how much to trust the output.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician reads an AI-generated summary and sees no warning about missing or incomplete data. They assume the summary is based on a full picture of the patient's history. They make a clinical decision based on an incomplete summary without realising it.
items.harm: The clinician makes a diagnosis or treatment decision based on incomplete information. Important conditions, medicines, or test results may have been missed by the AI tool. The patient could receive the wrong treatment, a delayed diagnosis, or miss a referral they need. This could cause serious or lasting harm.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The AI tool always shows a clear data completeness indicator on every clinical output, so the clinician can see at a glance how complete the underlying data is (DI-900CB621). The tool displays information about which patient group the summary is based on, including how many records were used, directly on the clinician-facing screen (DI-098D2C0D). When data from a small group of patients or low-confidence results are involved, the tool either hides the output or shows a clear low-confidence warning before the clinician sees it (DI-CB3DF3E1). The programme team sets the thresholds that decide when a warning is shown or an output is hidden, and reviews these settings regularly (DI-0D7DCC52). Before a clinician can act on a summary that has data gaps or coverage warnings, the tool requires them to actively confirm they have seen and understood the warning (DI-00E16F9E). The tool automatically detects when data is missing and always tells the clinician before they see any output that is based on incomplete records (DI-88F20177). A plain-English explanation of what the completeness indicator means is always available to the clinician in one click or tap (DI-B95A73E9). A short, clear disclaimer appears on every clinical intelligence panel at all times, reminding the clinician that the output is for information only (DI-E609C4E5). The confidence level the AI tool has in each interpretation it produces is shown alongside that interpretation on screen (DI-DA7584D8). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and user feedback every quarter to check that warnings are being displayed correctly and that clinicians are engaging with them.

items.title: The AI tool wrongly codes treatment plans or safety-netting advice as confirmed clinical findings
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads notes can misread sentences about future plans or warnings. For example, 'consider starting metformin' or 'call 999 if chest pain develops' describe things that have not happened yet. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible may label these as present findings. Those findings can then be saved into the patient record as if they were confirmed.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinical note contains treatment plans, safety-netting advice, or uncertain diagnostic statements. The AI tool reads these sentences and wrongly marks them as confirmed present findings. In the fully automated setting, the system saves these directly into the patient record without a clinician checking them. In the setting where a clinician reviews suggestions, the wrong suggestions still appear and waste the reviewer's time.
items.harm: A planned medicine may be coded as already prescribed. This creates a medicine safety risk if the patient has not yet started it. Safety-netting symptoms, such as chest pain to watch for, may be coded as findings the patient already has. This creates false diagnoses in the patient record. A speculative diagnosis may be coded as confirmed, leading to incorrect clinical decisions and potential patient harm.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The system uses rules to exclude treatment recommendations and diagnostic uncertainty from being coded as confirmed findings. These rules are built into the AI workflow and are reviewed by the clinical safety team at each software release (DI-A3107424). The system automatically suppresses alerts for safety-netting advice once a confirmed clinical response has been coded. This runs without manual input every time a record is updated (DI-0E215ADE). The system shows clinicians a plain-language summary of any coded finding before it is saved. This gives the reviewing clinician a clear chance to spot and reject incorrect suggestions at every review session (DI-66F1B177). A character-level locator ties each AI-extracted finding back to the exact words in the original note. This lets the reviewing clinician see the source sentence and judge whether the finding is real, every time a suggestion is made (DI-A0C90595). A configurable follow-up time window flags outstanding findings and places them on a worklist. The clinical team reviews this worklist at agreed intervals to catch any incorrectly coded items before they affect patient care (DI-4C73DC01). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

items.title: AD service account credential exposure
items.hazard: AD service account credentials are stored or emitted insecurely and accessed by an unauthorised actor.
items.hazardous_situation: Attacker uses the AD service account to enumerate groups, impersonate users, or pivot within the Trust's AD.
items.harm: Trust-wide IG / security incident extending well beyond MV Lite; IG breach.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Secure storage of AD service account credentials, obfuscated not plaintext; Windows DPAPI / .NET Data Protection equivalent (DI-MVL-005-004); configuration review at UAT; static analysis for plaintext credential patterns; minimum-necessary AD privilege.

items.title: Patient information sent to external AI services without confirmed data agreements
items.hazard: The system uses two AI services at the same time to check clinical notes. When the two services disagree, a third AI service is asked to decide. Each of these calls sends text from the patient's GP record to an external cloud service. This means patient-identifiable information may be sent to up to three external services for a single piece of clinical information.
items.hazardous_situation: The system tries to remove patient-identifiable information before sending notes to the AI services. However, there are known gaps in this process: some unusual formats of patient-identifiable information may not be caught and removed. Text that still contains patient details may then be sent to external cloud services. One service is based in the UK (AWS, London). Another is based in Sweden (Azure), which is lawful under UK data transfer rules for the European Economic Area. If a valid data processing agreement is not in place with each provider, this transfer may breach UK data protection law.
items.harm: A patient's confidential health information could be shared with an external company without proper legal agreements in place. This could breach the patient's right to confidentiality. It may also break UK data protection law (UK GDPR), which requires a completed Data Protection Impact Assessment before processing sensitive health data. The Information Commissioner's Office could investigate and issue a significant fine.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The system can be set to use only one AI service instead of two or three, reducing how many external services receive patient data. The clinical safety team can switch to single-service mode at any time (DI-80DD8A47). The system uses secure, time-limited access tokens to connect to each external service, so only authorised connections are made (DI-4DBE1A18). A separate test environment uses its own credentials and never handles real patient data, keeping live patient information away from testing activity (DI-2E40F292). The system flags data quality problems, including gaps in information removal, and records whether each check passed or failed so the team can review issues (DI-FC80B65A). Clinicians must actively confirm they have seen any warnings about data gaps before the system continues, creating a pause point if a problem is detected (DI-00E16F9E). Every clinical statement the system produces is linked back to the original source text in the patient record, so reviewers can check exactly what information was used (DI-740BE510). Reviewers can also select and highlight the exact section of the note the AI used, making it easier to spot if sensitive details were included (DI-E81545BE). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter. Additional controls are being identified.

items.title: Refile metadata misapplied -> wrong-patient attribution
items.hazard: Refile metadata applied incorrectly on a refiled document; refile provenance not shown, or document appears under wrong patient.
items.hazardous_situation: Clinician sees a document under the wrong patient context without the refile marker that would alert them.
items.harm: Wrong-patient clinical view; IG breach.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Refiled document provenance display - original Document ID and original MRN shown in list (DI-MVL-004-007); refile metadata ingestion during bulk load (DI-MVL-007-004); incremental refile bundle ingestion with provenance (DI-MVL-008-003).

items.title: Stale demographics undermine identity verification
items.hazard: HL7 ADT demographic update is lost, delayed, or misapplied; the demographic panel displays outdated data (e.g. old address, pre-marriage surname).
items.hazardous_situation: User performs demographic verification against stale data, verifies the wrong patient record, or fails to verify a legitimate patient.
items.harm: Patient misidentification (see R-MVL-001); refusal of care to a patient whose details have changed.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Demographic data reflects most recent HL7 ADT update (DI-MVL-003-003); last-synchronised timestamp on demographic panel (DI-MVL-003-004); HL7 demographic update processing (DI-MVL-008-002); sync monitoring and error logging (DI-MVL-008-006); proactive sync-failure alerting (new DI-MVL-008-007).

items.title: Unauthenticated access / authentication bypass
items.hazard: An endpoint serves PHI without enforcing authentication.
items.hazardous_situation: Anyone with Trust-network access (legitimate staff acting outside their role, or an attacker who has pivoted onto the network) can read PHI.
items.harm: IG breach; UK GDPR Article 32 violation; NHS DSP Toolkit failure.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Server-side authentication required for all application access (DI-MVL-005-001); Active Directory integration (DI-MVL-005-002); AD group-based access control (DI-MVL-005-003); authenticated-access restatements per data-exposing subsystem (DI-MVL-002-006, DI-MVL-003-005, DI-MVL-004-008, DI-MVL-006-008); pre-release security review and penetration test.

items.title: A clinician or trainee misreads the operations screen and either misses a quality alert or starts a live deployment too early.
items.hazard: The operations screen controls four key steps: training the AI, checking its quality, approving it, and making it live. Without clear labels and explanations, a less experienced user may not understand what each step does. They may accidentally close an important notice. They may also miss a status indicator if it relies on colour alone.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician or trainee with limited experience, reduced vision, or difficulty telling colours apart opens the operations screen. They see four unlabelled sections. They either ignore an unacknowledged quality alert, or they press 'Make it live' before the AI has finished training. This causes an unvalidated version of the AI to go live too soon.
items.harm: An AI that has not been properly checked starts adding clinical codes to patient records. Coding errors spread through records before anyone catches them. A missed quality alert means a pattern of incorrect coding continues for longer than it should.
items.mitigation_plan_description: First, the deployment status panel shows the current state of any approved change directly on the review screen. This stops a clinician from promoting an AI model before all steps are complete. The clinical safety team checks this panel is working at each deployment review (DI-6EA84931). Second, quality gates are set for each type of clinical relationship the AI learns. The AI cannot be made live unless it meets these quality thresholds. The clinical safety team reviews the gate settings at each model release (DI-80BD2F86). Third, if a quality alert is not acknowledged within the set time, the AI workflow pauses automatically. No further changes can be made until the alert is reviewed. The clinical safety committee checks that this automatic pause is triggering correctly every quarter (DI-5A802C83). Fourth, historical coding frequency data is shown on the coding review screen. This helps a reviewer spot unusual patterns quickly, even if they are less experienced. The clinical safety team audits this display during quarterly case record reviews (DI-22F4E3CE). Fifth, the data quality engine applies configurable rules to each patient episode and records whether each rule passed or failed, along with a suggested fix. This gives reviewers a clear, plain-language summary of any problems. The clinical safety committee reviews rule performance and remediation rates every quarter (DI-FC80B65A). The clinical safety committee reviews all five controls together every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

items.title: A junior trainee misunderstands unclear review screen labels and suppresses a real clinical finding
items.hazard: The coding-review screen asks the reviewer to accept the AI tool's suggestion, choose a different clinical code, or suppress the finding so it never appears again. Each choice saves a change to the patient record. The screen uses terms that a junior or non-clinical reviewer may not understand. Without plain-language explanations, the reviewer may not know what they are agreeing to.
items.hazardous_situation: A trainee opens the coding-review screen. They see a case where the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible has marked the finding as 'declined', and the suggested clinical code does not match the expected category. The trainee does not understand either term. To clear the case from their queue, they click 'Suppress'. The finding was a real clinical event that should have been coded. It is now hidden from all future AI workflow runs.
items.harm: A real clinical finding is permanently hidden from the patient record. The patient may miss follow-up care. The finding will also be absent from care audit records, creating a gap that could affect the patient's ongoing treatment.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the coding-review card shows the reviewer the exact text from the notes that the AI tool used to reach its decision, alongside a plain-language label saying whether the finding was judged to be present, absent, or possible. This helps the reviewer understand what they are being asked to confirm. The development team builds this into the review screen (DI-375C7EB1). Second, every coded finding on the review card includes a plain-English explanation of what the clinical code means and why the AI tool suggested it. This is displayed automatically each time a reviewer opens a case. The development team builds this into the product (DI-66F1B177). Third, the AI workflow applies confidence thresholds that vary by the type and category of finding. Findings that score below the threshold for their category are not presented for suppression without an additional prompt. The development team configures these thresholds and reviews them when the AI tool is updated (DI-F0B8A7B0). Fourth, every accept, override, or suppress action is recorded in a full audit trail. The clinical safety team can review who made each decision and on what basis, without accessing the wider patient record. This log is available at any time (DI-09E26C1D). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all four controls are working as intended every quarter.

items.title: A patient or clinician on a touch screen taps the wrong button because touch targets are too small
items.hazard: The system shows buttons and list rows that can be too small to tap accurately. On a phone or tablet, a patient, carer, or clinician with mild hand tremor can easily tap the wrong control. This risk is higher when the user is a child, an older person, or a carer under stress.
items.hazardous_situation: A patient opens their safety-netting advice on a phone and tries to tap the confirmation button. Instead they tap the NHS 111 contact button just below it. This sends a false alert, or the patient never reads the red-flag warning list. Separately, a clinician reviewing a list of clinical codes accidentally approves the wrong code because the rows are too close together.
items.harm: The patient is sent down the wrong care pathway. Or an incorrect clinical code is saved into the patient record and passed on to other systems. Both errors could delay the right diagnosis or trigger the wrong clinical action.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Every safety-netting action is recorded automatically with the clinician's identity and the exact time it happened. This means any mis-tap can be identified and reviewed. The clinical safety team checks these records regularly (DI-B46AD5CE). When a patient-facing step fails or is completed incorrectly, the system adds that encounter to a failed list. A clinician can review it and re-run the step with one click, correcting any error before it affects care (DI-69CE20C1). The system also records a clear, machine-readable reason for every error. This helps the safety team spot patterns of mis-taps quickly and act on them (DI-6654FB0E). A plain-language explanation of what each action means is always available to the patient or clinician in one tap, reducing the chance they act without understanding (DI-B95A73E9). Any change to safety-netting guidance is managed through a controlled registry. The safety team is alerted when guidance changes, so they can check whether touch-target risks need to be reassessed (DI-ED3A89F5). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and error reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

items.title: A patient record shows an active care pathway when the condition is absent or historical
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads notes can find mentions of conditions that are recorded as absent, ruled out, or historical. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible must filter these out before creating a care pathway record. If this filtering fails, the system creates an active pathway record based on a condition the patient does not currently have.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician writes "no evidence of cancer" or "history of breast cancer (resolved)". The AI tool that reads notes correctly finds the cancer mention but the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible does not filter it out. The system then creates an active cancer pathway record for that patient. A dashboard shows the patient as being on an active cancer pathway. A clinician may then arrange unnecessary follow-up or investigations for a condition the patient does not have.
items.harm: A clinician may act on an incorrect active pathway record and arrange unnecessary tests or treatment for a patient who does not have the condition. Equally, if the filtering is set too broadly, real active pathways may be hidden, and a patient who needs follow-up may be missed. Both errors could cause the patient direct harm.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The system stores the exact words from the notes alongside every decision the AI tool makes about whether a condition is present, absent, or possible. This lets a clinician or reviewer check why a pathway record was created (DI-23822663). The coding review card shows the clinician the AI tool's decision and the supporting words from the notes, so errors can be spotted quickly during routine review (DI-375C7EB1). The AI workflow uses multi-type classification to handle overlapping clinical codes correctly, reducing the chance of a wrong pathway record being created in the first place (DI-DC61F5B6). Any pathway record that is flagged as potentially incorrect is blocked from appearing in reports until a clinician has reviewed and resolved the flag, preventing incorrect information from reaching clinical dashboards (DI-A0579B64). The system uses an up-to-date clinical coding reference so that code meanings are current and correctly interpreted (DI-553F50A2). A workflow is in place to manage changes to clinical coding releases and resolve any conflicts before they affect pathway records (DI-B193C816). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flagged pathway records every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

items.title: A patient visit is assigned to the wrong audit programme
items.hazard: The AI tool that sorts patient visits into audit programmes may place a visit in the wrong programme. This can happen when two programmes overlap and the AI is not sure which one applies.
items.hazardous_situation: A patient visit is filed under the wrong audit programme. The clinician reviewing that programme does not see the visit. The correct programme misses the visit entirely. The patient's care need goes unreviewed.
items.harm: The patient does not receive the review or follow-up linked to the correct audit programme. A clinical need, such as a long-term condition check or a medicines review, may be missed. This could lead to delayed diagnosis or a gap in ongoing care.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Six controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool that sorts visits uses a fixed set of managed rules and must pass a test before any decision is saved to the patient record. This test runs automatically every time a visit is classified (DI-8CE01B3E). Second, when a clinician spots a wrong classification, they can label it as incorrect. The AI tool learns from these corrections and the updated model is recorded in a central register. The clinical informatics team reviews labelled errors on an ongoing basis (DI-0ADE6A8E). Third, the rules that define each audit programme can be adjusted by a clinical lead without needing a software release. This means errors in programme boundaries can be fixed quickly (DI-AA8014F9). Fourth, the settings for each audit programme can be updated from data alone, again without a software release, so the team can respond rapidly to any drift in how visits are being sorted (DI-CD931485). Fifth, the AI workflow monitors how often clinical codes appear for each type of patient entry. If the pattern drifts beyond a set limit, an alert is raised for the clinical safety team to investigate. This check runs continuously (DI-37315D03). Sixth, the AI tool shows its confidence level next to every classification it produces. A clinician can see at a glance when the AI is uncertain and apply their own judgement before accepting the result (DI-DA7584D8). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, labelled errors, and drift alerts every quarter to confirm all six controls are working as intended.

items.title: A patient, carer, or junior staff member acts on a screen they do not fully understand because no plain-English explanation is shown, leading to a wrong or missed action
items.hazard: The system shows clinical terms such as 'microalbuminuria' (protein in the urine) and 'HbA1c' (a blood sugar test) without explaining what they mean. There are no plain-English labels telling the user why they are on a screen or what they should do next. Patients, carers, and new staff may guess the meaning or ignore the information entirely.
items.hazardous_situation: A carer reads a safety-netting message saying 'persistent haematuria (blood in the urine) should be reviewed'. The carer does not recognise the word and assumes it does not apply. They close the screen. The patient does not get the follow-up the clinical team intended. Separately, a junior coder sees a record marked in a way they do not understand and approves it without realising the original diagnosis was overturned. Incorrect clinical information then moves forward through the system.
items.harm: A patient misses an important safety-netting prompt and does not receive timely follow-up care. Incorrect clinical information is passed on, causing the patient to be directed to the wrong care pathway. Both situations can lead to delayed diagnosis or inappropriate treatment.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The system records every safety-netting action, including who took it and when, so that nothing can be silently missed or altered. This log is maintained automatically by the system at all times (DI-B46AD5CE). The system keeps a worklist of all safety-netting items that have not yet been acted on. The clinical team reviews this worklist regularly to spot any outstanding items (DI-4C73DC01). When a clinician records a confirmed clinical response, the system automatically removes the related alert from the worklist. This stops the same item being acted on twice or left open in error. The system does this without any manual step (DI-0E215ADE). The worklist can be filtered by how serious an item is, how many days it has been outstanding, and which group of patients it relates to. This helps the clinical team prioritise the most urgent items quickly (DI-520A8674). Patient information and clinical reference information are held in separate parts of the system. This reduces the risk that a display error in one area affects the other (DI-84F44836). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter. Additional controls to address plain-English labelling and in-screen guidance are being identified.

items.title: A quality problem in a patient episode is not caught by the checking rules
items.hazard: The system checks each patient episode for quality problems before using it in reports. The set of checking rules may not cover every type of problem. Some quality problems could pass through undetected.
items.hazardous_situation: A patient episode with a quality problem is not flagged. It is included in clinical reports or pathway decisions. Clinicians act on information that is incomplete or wrong.
items.harm: A clinician makes a care decision based on a flawed patient record. The patient may receive the wrong treatment, miss a needed referral, or have a serious condition overlooked. This could cause serious harm.
items.mitigation_plan_description: First, any episode the system marks as having a quality problem is blocked from reports until a clinician or administrator resolves the problem. This happens automatically every time an episode is processed (DI-A0579B64). Second, the system checks each episode for unusual durations, missing steps, and events recorded in the wrong order. These checks run automatically on every episode (DI-1206D9E8). Third, the system flags any part of a record it is not confident about, and highlights where clinical codes within the same episode contradict each other. This runs automatically during every episode review (DI-C7A810AA). Fourth, clinical teams can update the set of checking rules for their programme without needing a software release. A named administrator applies updates whenever guidelines change (DI-AA8014F9). Fifth, the system tells the reviewer whether each episode was classified by fixed rules or by the AI tool that reads notes, so the reviewer knows how much to rely on the result. This is shown automatically on every episode (DI-8C236A1A). Sixth, when a clinician corrects a clinical code, the system checks that related codes and terms are still consistent. This check runs automatically at the point of correction (DI-1B8AC856). Seventh, the system compares the clinical codes produced by the AI tool that reads notes against those produced by the AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible. Any disagreement is flagged for review. This runs automatically on every episode (DI-F298AE65). Eighth, before any new set of checking rules is switched on, the system runs a test pass on real data without making any changes. A named administrator must approve the results before the rules go live (DI-ACB587DD). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flagging rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

items.title: A reviewer picks the wrong clinical code when correcting a patient record
items.hazard: When a clinician reviews and corrects clinical codes in a patient record, they may choose the wrong replacement code. This can happen when the correct code requires specialist terminology knowledge they do not have, or when the original note is ambiguous.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician approves an incorrect clinical code during a coding correction review. The patient record then holds the wrong diagnosis or condition code. Future clinical decisions, referrals, or medicines may be based on that wrong code without anyone realising the error.
items.harm: The patient's record contains the wrong diagnosis or condition. A doctor or nurse reading the record may make the wrong clinical decision. This could lead to the patient receiving the wrong treatment, missing a needed treatment, or being referred along the wrong care pathway. The harm could be serious.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Five controls reduce this risk. First, the system checks that any proposed replacement code is consistent with related codes already in the record and flags conflicts for the reviewer to consider before approving (DI-1B8AC856). This check runs automatically every time a coding correction is reviewed. Second, the AI tool that reads clinical notes is designed to preserve important detail such as whether a condition is confirmed, suspected, or ruled out, so the replacement code options shown to the reviewer reflect the correct clinical meaning (DI-6A0B55A4). This runs automatically during every AI workflow. Third, the system checks that any proposed replacement code is current and valid in the clinical coding system before showing it to the reviewer, so out-of-date or retired codes cannot be selected (DI-26CBDB16). This check runs automatically for every proposed code. Fourth, the review screen shows the reviewer how often each code has been used historically for similar patients, giving useful context to support the decision (DI-22F4E3CE). This information is displayed automatically on every coding correction review page. Fifth, the AI workflow can use two independent AI models and only suggests a replacement code when both models agree, reducing the chance of a misleading suggestion reaching the reviewer (DI-80DD8A47). This is configured by the system administrator and runs during every AI workflow. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reviewer feedback every quarter to confirm all five controls are working as intended.

items.title: A rule set too broadly stops a clinical term from being coded at all
items.hazard: A reviewer creates a rule that tells the AI workflow to ignore a clinical term everywhere in the notes. The rule should only apply in specific situations, such as when a patient is awaiting an appointment or when the term is used hypothetically. Because no limiting phrase is added, the rule removes the term from coding in every situation, including when it is genuinely present.
items.hazardous_situation: The rule silently removes all future mentions of the term before any clinician sees them. The term simply stops appearing in the review queue. No one is alerted. The gap in coding is invisible because there is nothing missing to notice.
items.harm: A clinical condition such as hypertension (high blood pressure), diabetes review, or a biopsy result is consistently not coded across many patients. Audit figures show artificially low numbers of cases. Decisions about service planning and quality improvement are based on this incomplete data. Future patients may receive the wrong level of care as a result.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce the chance of this harm reaching patients. First, the AI tool that reads notes and the AI tool that decides whether something is present, absent, or possible are compared automatically after every processing run. If their results disagree for a given clinical term, the system flags the difference for review by the clinical informatics team (DI-F298AE65). Second, the system flags any clinical term it is not confident about, and it also flags when two coding decisions within the same patient episode contradict each other. A clinician reviewer checks these flags daily (DI-C7A810AA). Third, the AI workflow tracks how often each type of clinical term is coded over time. If the coding rate for any term drops below a set threshold, the system raises an alert to the clinical safety team. The safety team reviews these drift reports at least weekly (DI-37315D03). Fourth, all rules that control how the AI codes terms are held in a monitored registry under clinical change control. Any change to a rule must be approved before it goes live, and the full context of any alert is recorded. The clinical safety officer oversees this process and reviews the registry monthly (DI-ED3A89F5). All corrections made by reviewers in the unified review queue are stored as structured examples to improve future AI behaviour (DI-890BE989). The clinical safety committee reviews evidence that all four controls are working every quarter.

items.title: A single reviewer approves a wrong clinical code for a common phrase, causing every future patient record with that phrase to be coded incorrectly.
items.hazard: When a reviewer links a phrase to a clinical code, the AI tool saves that link and uses it automatically for every future patient record containing the same phrase. If the reviewer picks the wrong code, no second check happens. Every record with that phrase is then coded incorrectly until someone notices.
items.hazardous_situation: A reviewer links the phrase 'chest tightness' to the clinical code for anxiety instead of angina. The AI tool immediately saves this link. All future patient records containing 'chest tightness' are automatically coded as anxiety. Patients with possible heart symptoms are miscoded for weeks until a routine audit spots the pattern.
items.harm: Many patient records carry the wrong clinical code for the same phrase. Patients with that phrase may be sent down the wrong care pathway, receive the wrong clinical decisions, or be missed when the system searches for patients with a specific condition such as angina.
items.mitigation_plan_description: First, the system holds any new phrase-to-code link in a staging area before it goes live. A second reviewer must approve the change, and the system keeps a full version history so any wrong link can be rolled back quickly (DI-9FD54AD6). The clinical safety team checks this gate is working every quarter. Second, when a reviewer is deciding on a code, the screen shows how many patient records use that phrase. This helps the reviewer understand the impact of their choice before approving it. The system also blocks duplicate links from being created (DI-30D95132). Third, every coded entry in a patient record keeps a clear link back to the original note and the source of the code. This makes it straightforward to trace and correct a wrong code if one is found (DI-740BE510). Fourth, the AI tool cannot publish any coded interpretation without a reviewer making an active decision. No code reaches a patient record without human sign-off (DI-604767B1). Fifth, the review screen shows whether a change has already been deployed to live records. Reviewers can see the potential reach of a decision before they approve it (DI-6EA84931). Sixth, the review screen shows which patient records and phrases depend on the link being changed. Reviewers can see the full impact before approving (DI-4221A226). Seventh, after codes are saved to patient records, an automated check runs to flag any coded entries that do not match accepted clinical guidelines. This catches patterns of miscoding early (DI-2AFF691F). The clinical safety committee reviews audit results from all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

items.title: A task needing urgent action is hidden from the clinician's view
items.hazard: The system shows each user only the tasks linked to their chosen role. A clinician who also covers other duties may have a safety alert waiting in a different part of the system. That alert is tucked away in a secondary area the clinician does not normally open. The clinician does not see it and does not act on it.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician signs in and selects the clinician role. A safety alert has been assigned to them via the staff work queue. That queue does not appear in the clinician's main menu. The clinician finishes their session without ever seeing the alert.
items.harm: A safety-netting action is not completed on time. The patient's follow-up or investigation is delayed. This could cause harm if the finding was serious and needed prompt action.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce the chance that a missed alert leads to patient harm. First, the system keeps a permanent record of every safety-netting action, including who acted and when, so nothing can be quietly lost (DI-B46AD5CE). The clinical safety team reviews these records regularly to spot gaps. Second, the system automatically closes an alert only when a confirmed clinical response has been recorded in the patient record, so an alert cannot disappear just because time has passed (DI-0E215ADE). Third, the system holds a worklist of all outstanding flagged findings that have not been acted on within the set time window. This worklist is checked by the team responsible for safety netting (DI-4C73DC01). Fourth, that worklist can be filtered by how serious the finding is, how many days it has been waiting, and which group of patients it affects, making it easier for a reviewer to spot overdue alerts quickly (DI-520A8674). A plain-language explanation of what the coverage indicator means is available in one step, so any clinician who is unsure what they are looking at can get help immediately (DI-B95A73E9). The clinical safety committee reviews whether all five controls are working as intended every quarter.

items.title: AI tool gives an inaccurate or misleading interpretation of a clinical finding
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads and summarises clinical codes can produce an interpretation that is factually wrong or misleading. This can happen when the AI generates plausible-sounding text that does not match the actual coded finding in the patient record.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews the AI-generated summary of a patient's coded findings. The summary contains an inaccurate or misleading statement. The clinician, under time pressure, accepts the summary without checking the underlying record. They base a clinical decision on the incorrect information.
items.harm: The clinician makes a wrong or delayed clinical decision because the AI summary misrepresented the patient's condition. This could lead to the wrong treatment being given, a needed treatment being missed, or a serious condition being overlooked. The patient could suffer serious harm as a result.
items.mitigation_plan_description: First, the AI tool is designed to summarise only the structured facts already recorded in the patient record. It cannot add diagnoses or treatment recommendations of its own. This keeps the summary anchored to what is actually documented (DI-69C29EEF). The AI tool team sets and maintains this boundary. Second, the AI tool does not include diagnostic or treatment recommendations in any interpretation it produces. This reduces the risk that a clinician acts on AI-generated clinical advice rather than their own judgement (DI-A3107424). The AI tool team enforces this at the design level. Third, every AI-generated interpretation is written in plain language so the reviewing clinician can quickly check it against the original coded finding (DI-66F1B177). The AI tool produces this plain-language version automatically for every summary. Fourth, the AI tool displays a confidence level alongside every interpretation it generates. A lower confidence level prompts the clinician to check the source record before acting (DI-DA7584D8). This is shown automatically each time a summary is presented. Fifth, no AI-generated interpretation is published to the patient record or shared with a clinician until a human reviewer has made an explicit decision to approve it. The system blocks publication until this step is completed (DI-604767B1). The reviewing clinician carries out this check every time. Sixth, an automated check runs on each coded encounter to assess whether the AI interpretation follows accepted clinical guidelines. Any interpretation that does not conform is flagged before the reviewer sees it (DI-2AFF691F). This check runs automatically as part of the AI workflow. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reviewer decisions every quarter to confirm all controls are working as intended.

items.title: Active cancer investigation wrongly closed because an unrelated test result is misread by the AI tool
items.hazard: A clinical code meaning 'no evidence of cancer found' is used in many different situations. It can appear after a cervical smear, a routine health check, or a cancer pathway discharge. The AI tool that reads notes may search for this code across the whole patient record without checking the date. If it finds the code from an unrelated test, it can wrongly decide that an open cancer investigation has been resolved.
items.hazardous_situation: A patient has an open urgent two-week-wait breast cancer investigation started in July 2024. In 2026, a cervical smear result is recorded using the same clinical code for 'no cancer found'. Because the AI tool does not check whether the code relates to the breast investigation, it closes the breast investigation and marks it as resolved. The breast investigation disappears from the open cases dashboard. Clinicians reviewing open cancer cases can no longer see it.
items.harm: The active breast cancer investigation is wrongly marked as finished. It is removed from the clinician review list. The patient may not receive timely follow-up. This increases the risk of a delayed cancer diagnosis, which could cause serious harm.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the AI tool that decides if a finding is present, absent, or possible displays its reasoning and the supporting evidence on a coding review card, so a clinician can see why the investigation was closed (DI-375C7EB1). This check runs each time the AI tool processes a patient record. Second, the system shows a plain-English summary of what each coded finding means, so reviewers can quickly spot if a code has been applied in the wrong context (DI-66F1B177). This is shown to the reviewing clinician every time a coded finding is displayed. Third, any episode the AI tool has flagged as uncertain is blocked from being reported as closed until a clinician resolves the flag (DI-A0579B64). This quality gate runs automatically before any episode status is finalised. Fourth, when clinical guidelines that underpin the AI rules are updated or withdrawn, the system enforces a review of all episodes that relied on those rules, preventing outdated rules from silently closing investigations (DI-F1A768AE). This runs whenever a guideline change is recorded. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and flag resolution rates every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

items.title: Analysis of too few patients produces misleading results that a clinician acts on
items.hazard: The tool analyses patient data to find patterns and group patients into pathways. If the underlying data is incomplete or covers too few patients, the results can look reliable but are not. A clinician or service lead may then make a care or pathway decision based on figures that do not reflect reality.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician or service lead runs a pathway analysis on a small group of patients, for example fewer than 30 patients over three months. The tool returns a clear, confident-sounding result. No warning appears to say the data is too thin to trust. The user redesigns a service or changes how patients are triaged based on this result.
items.harm: A service change or patient routing decision is made on unreliable evidence. This could delay care, send patients down the wrong pathway, or cause harm by deprioritising patients who need urgent attention.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The tool shows a data coverage indicator in the research workspace whenever results are based on limited data. This warns the user before they act on the findings (DI-93162C3C). The AI workflow automatically detects gaps in the data and must display a clear warning on any clinician-facing result that is based on incomplete information. This runs every time a result is produced (DI-88F20177). Every clinician-facing output includes a prominent indicator showing how complete and reliable the underlying data is. The clinical team reviews this indicator as part of normal use (DI-900CB621). Each output also shows details about the patient group it is based on, including how many patients were included and over what time period. This helps the user judge whether the result can be trusted (DI-098D2C0D). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

items.title: Automated quality checks miss incorrectly coded clinical entries
items.hazard: The system uses automated rules to check that clinical codes in patient records are correct. These rules have gaps. Some incorrect codes pass through the checks without being flagged for a clinician to review.
items.hazardous_situation: A patient's record contains an incorrect clinical code. The automated quality checks do not catch it. The code enters the patient's care record without any clinician reviewing it. Clinical decisions or care pathways may then be based on wrong information.
items.harm: A clinician makes a clinical decision based on an incorrect code in the patient's record. The patient receives the wrong treatment, misses a needed treatment, or is placed on the wrong care pathway. This could cause serious harm.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the system blocks any flagged episode from being used in reports until a clinician has reviewed and resolved the flag. This runs automatically every time an episode is processed (DI-A0579B64). Second, a human-review gate stops any unreviewed episode classification from being used in audit reports. The clinical team manages this gate as part of routine reporting (DI-BD696225). Third, the system automatically checks coded patient encounters against clinical guideline rules. This runs each time a new coded entry is saved (DI-2AFF691F). Fourth, the programme team can update the guideline rule set at any time without needing a software release. This means gaps in the rules can be fixed quickly when found (DI-AA8014F9). The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working every quarter.

items.title: Clinician makes an accidental or missed action in the coding review screen due to unclear warnings, hidden errors, or access barriers
items.hazard: The coding review screen lets clinicians remove clinical codes, dismiss suggestions, or reset all work with a single click. There is no confirmation step before these actions take effect. When the system fails to load data, the screen looks the same as when there is genuinely nothing to review. Some clinicians using a keyboard may trigger actions by accident.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician clicks Remove, Dismiss, Create ignore rule, or Reset all without meaning to. The action happens immediately and is hard to undo. Separately, the system fails silently: the review queue appears empty, but this is because the system has not loaded properly, not because there is nothing to review. A clinician using only a keyboard may press a shortcut key by accident and reject a suggestion without intending to.
items.harm: A correct clinical code may be deleted by accident. A broad ignore rule may be created, causing the system to suppress correct codes in future. Clinicians may skip the review queue believing it is empty, when in fact the system has failed to load outstanding work. Any of these errors could lead to clinical codes being missed or removed from patient records, distorting the clinical picture and audit data, and potentially affecting patient care decisions.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Role-based access control limits which clinicians can take destructive actions such as removing codes or creating ignore rules. Only authorised users can finalise or change AI suggestions. The system enforces this automatically on every action (DI-E83828A9). When a clinician corrects a suggestion, the system resets the confirmation step and requires the clinician to actively re-confirm before the change is saved. This stops accidental single-click changes from taking effect without a second check (DI-5ADEC3D1). When the system fails to load data, a dedicated failed-encounter list shows the clinician which records could not be loaded and why. A one-click option lets the clinician re-queue those records immediately, so a failed load is never mistaken for an empty queue (DI-69CE20C1). When a system component returns an error, the system records a structured error code rather than showing a blank screen. This means failures can be detected and investigated rather than going unnoticed (DI-6654FB0E). All review actions are recorded in a full audit trail. The safety team can check this trail to see whether accidental actions have occurred and whether failed loads were detected and resolved (DI-09E26C1D). The review screen shows how often a clinical code has been used historically. This gives the clinician a prompt to pause before removing an unusual or infrequent code, reducing the chance of accidental deletion (DI-22F4E3CE). The clinical safety committee reviews audit trail reports and failed-encounter logs every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

items.title: Clinicians or patients with visual or vestibular conditions cannot safely read clinical information shown by the system
items.hazard: The system displays some text very small — around 10 pixels — and uses light grey text on a white background. The contrast between the text and background is too low to meet accessibility standards. Moving images on screen cannot be turned off. This means clinicians with age-related sight loss, colour-blindness, or low vision may not be able to read important clinical information clearly. Patients who are sensitive to screen movement may look away before reading safety advice fully.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician with age-related macular degeneration reviews a list of coded patient encounters. Small grey labels show whether a finding is confirmed, absent, or possible. The text is tiny and the contrast is poor. The clinician misses a label showing a finding is absent and approves the record as if the finding is present. This incorrect entry then carries forward into the patient record. Separately, a patient with a vestibular condition — one that causes dizziness or nausea from movement — tries to read safety advice on screen. An animated banner is running and cannot be stopped. The patient looks away and does not take in the advice.
items.harm: A clinician makes a clinical decision based on information they misread or missed entirely. A patient does not absorb safety advice because they could not read it comfortably. For older patients, children, and patients with a disability, the system may be effectively unusable. This creates a direct patient safety risk and may also breach the Equality Act 2010.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The following controls are in place to reduce this risk. The system automatically suppresses alerts when a confirmed clinical response has already been coded, reducing the number of small status labels a clinician must read at once (DI-0E215ADE). This control is built into the system and runs automatically every time the system processes a coded encounter. The system flags outputs where confidence is low or the patient group is small, so clinicians are prompted to look more carefully before acting (DI-CB3DF3E1). This control runs automatically as part of the AI workflow each time results are generated. The system produces a structured written summary drawn from coded encounters, the patient's pathway stage, and any safety alerts, giving clinicians a clear plain-text overview that does not rely on small labels alone (DI-30D9CC61). This summary is generated automatically each time a relevant encounter is reviewed. The system shows how often a clinical code has been used historically on the coding review page, helping clinicians spot unusual or unexpected entries that may reflect a misread label (DI-22F4E3CE). This is displayed automatically during coding correction review. The system builds episode records from related encounters in a consistent, rule-based way, reducing the chance that a misread label leads to a structurally incorrect record (DI-FF9C74E2). This runs automatically each time a new episode is constructed. The clinical safety committee reviews whether these controls are working effectively every quarter. Additional controls specifically addressing font size, contrast ratios, and motion settings are being identified and will be added to this risk record once confirmed.

items.title: Clinicians using assistive technology cannot tell where they are in the system or read status alerts correctly
items.hazard: The system does not tell screen readers which page is currently open. The logo cannot be activated using a keyboard alone. The organisation selector has no label that a screen reader can announce. Status dots use colour only to show whether something is healthy or has an error. Confirmation dialogs do not describe what the clinician is agreeing to. Together, these gaps mean clinicians who rely on assistive technology cannot safely orient themselves or spot critical alerts during clinical tasks.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician using a screen reader opens the encounter review page and wants to go to the Audit section. Because the system does not announce which page is currently open, they navigate to the wrong section and work on the wrong group of patients. They approve records that do not belong to the correct context. Separately, a clinician with colour blindness cannot tell a healthy status dot from an error status dot on a pathway dashboard and misses a clinical alert.
items.harm: Clinical decisions may be made against the wrong group of patients. Alerts may be missed by clinicians with visual impairment. Safety-netting confirmations may be submitted without the clinician understanding what they are agreeing to. Each of these outcomes could lead to delayed or incorrect care for patients.
items.mitigation_plan_description: A deployment status panel shows the current state of approved changes and is visible from the review interface. This helps clinicians confirm they are working in the correct context before acting (DI-6EA84931). The clinical safety team checks this panel is present and correct as part of each approved change review. Safety-netting actions are recorded permanently with the clinician's identity and the time they were taken. This creates an auditable trail so any action taken in the wrong context can be identified and corrected (DI-B46AD5CE). The clinical safety team reviews these records regularly to spot patterns of error. Automatic alert suppression activates only after a confirmed coded clinical response has been recorded. This reduces the risk that an alert is silently missed because a status dot was misread (DI-0E215ADE). The clinical safety team checks suppression events each quarter to confirm they are triggered correctly. The AI-generated structured summary brings together coded encounters, pathway stage, and safety-netting alerts in one place. This gives clinicians a text-based overview that does not rely on colour alone (DI-30D9CC61). The clinical safety committee reviews whether this summary is being used and whether it is reducing missed alerts, every quarter. Reference ranges and review status are shown in the content currency dashboard. This provides an additional text-based check that does not depend on colour coding (DI-E7609DD8). The clinical safety committee reviews this dashboard quarterly to confirm it remains current and accessible. Additional controls to address the underlying accessibility gaps in the interface are being identified.

items.title: Dashboard counts the wrong group of patients as its baseline population
items.hazard: The dashboard works out how many patients should be on a care pathway by counting all registered patients. It does not remove patients who are not eligible for that pathway. This means the baseline number used for all calculations is wrong from the start.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews the dashboard to check how well their practice is managing a care pathway. The baseline population figure is too large because ineligible patients have not been removed. The percentage of patients meeting targets looks better than it really is. The clinician believes care is on track and does not act.
items.harm: Patients who need review or treatment are not identified. The clinician does not follow up with them. Those patients may miss timely diagnosis or treatment, leading to serious harm from delayed care.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce this risk.
