First, the dashboard shows national benchmark figures alongside the practice figures so clinicians can spot when their results look unusually good or bad compared with peers across the country. The development team sets this up at build and the clinical safety committee checks it is working each quarter (DI-BA2C8F3E). Second, the dashboard includes a deprivation analysis panel that breaks down pathway performance by local deprivation level. If the denominator is wrong, the breakdown will look inconsistent and prompt investigation. The clinical lead reviews this panel at each monthly governance meeting (DI-94359E76). Third, the waiting-time performance panel highlights breaches and lets clinicians drill down into individual patient lists. If the denominator is inflated, breach rates will appear lower than expected and the drill-down will reveal patients who should not be included. Clinicians use this panel during weekly operational reviews (DI-35494904). Fourth, the guided population research workspace lets clinicians build their own plain-English searches to cross-check the dashboard population against their own criteria. Any mismatch between the dashboard count and the clinician's own search will flag a denominator problem. Clinicians can run this check at any time (DI-DD67ACFF). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and benchmark comparisons every quarter to confirm all four controls remain effective.

items.title: Errors in the examples used to teach the AI cause it to suggest wrong clinical codes
items.hazard: The AI learns to recognise conditions in patient notes by studying checked examples. Two faults can corrupt these examples. First, if a clinician edits the source text after marking it up, the marked positions can shift and point to the wrong words. Second, if examples showing that a condition is absent or not confirmed are left in the teaching set by mistake, the AI learns to treat absent conditions as present. Both faults can reach the AI training process uncorrected.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinical informatician reviews and edits patient notes used to teach the AI. After editing, the position markers for clinical terms can drift and point to the wrong characters. Separately, examples where a condition was recorded as absent, not confirmed, or belonging to a family member are not removed before training begins. Both types of faulty example are included in the next AI training run. The AI then learns incorrect boundaries for clinical terms and may treat conditions the patient does not have as if they are present, or miss conditions that are genuinely present.
items.harm: The AI suggests wrong clinical codes to clinical staff. Conditions the patient does not have may appear as present diagnoses. Conditions the patient does have may be missed. This can lead to incorrect disease registers, missed Quality and Outcomes Framework (QOF) coding, and inaccurate clinical summaries seen by doctors and nurses caring for the patient.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce this risk. First, every clinical term pulled from a patient note is stored with a permanent, unbreakable link back to the exact source text it came from, so any drift in position can be detected before training begins; the engineering team applies this automatically every time examples are prepared (DI-B2512CB3). Second, when a reviewer selects a clinical term to mark up, the tool highlights the exact words in the source note so the reviewer can immediately see if the position is wrong; reviewers use this check during every curation session (DI-E81545BE). Third, when the AI pulls a clinical term from a note it records a confidence score and full details of where the term came from; the clinical safety team inspects these records to spot patterns of error before any training run is approved (DI-31126C6C). Fourth, the process that converts checked examples into the training format preserves every label without loss, so faults are not introduced at the final export step; the engineering team validates this at each export (DI-6EFD68D0). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs from all four controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended. Additional controls are being identified.

items.title: Missing or wrong links between clinical findings lead to incorrect coding suggestions
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads notes can attach negation or context to the wrong clinical finding. This happens when the link between two related findings is missing or uses an unsupported type. The result is that the AI misreads what the notes actually say.
items.hazardous_situation: A reviewer connects a finding to an unsupported target, or a link between related findings is not saved correctly. The AI workflow then treats those findings as separate, unrelated facts. It suggests an incorrect clinical code based on that misreading.
items.harm: An incorrect clinical code can place a patient on the wrong care pathway. It can also distort disease reporting and mislead the reviewing clinician. This may delay recognition of a serious clinical condition.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The AI follows a strict set of rules that only allows supported, valid links between clinical findings. This stops unsupported connections from being made in the first place (DI-3EA60D5A). The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible is limited to working only with structured, confirmed facts from the notes. It cannot draw on information outside those facts (DI-69C29EEF). Every clinical statement carries a record of where it came from and which clinical code it is linked to. This lets reviewers trace any suggestion back to its source (DI-740BE510). The system classifies overlapping clinical findings separately, so one finding does not incorrectly absorb the meaning of another (DI-DC61F5B6). When a reviewer selects a finding, the system highlights the exact words in the original notes that the AI used. The reviewer can then check the AI has read the context correctly (DI-E81545BE). The system compares results against reference ranges and assigns a severity band, flagging findings that may need urgent attention (DI-21E93377). Alerts are automatically suppressed once a clinician has confirmed a coded response, reducing noise for the reviewer (DI-0E215ADE). Every action a clinician takes is saved with their identity and a timestamp. This record cannot be altered (DI-B46AD5CE). Reviewers can filter their worklist by severity, how long a finding has been outstanding, and patient group. This helps them prioritise the most important cases (DI-520A8674). The system maintains a worklist of findings that have not yet been followed up, within a time window that can be adjusted for local needs (DI-4C73DC01). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and worklist data every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

items.title: Patient missed by the system and not invited to the programme
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads clinical notes may fail to recognise a relevant encounter. Separately, the system may fail to build a complete clinical episode from those encounters. Either failure can mean the system does not flag the patient for the programme.
items.hazardous_situation: A patient who should be invited to the programme is not identified. The system does not add them to the shortlist. No clinician is alerted. The patient receives no invitation and misses the care pathway.
items.harm: The patient does not receive timely assessment or treatment through the programme. A serious or worsening condition may go undetected. This could lead to significant harm, including delayed diagnosis or avoidable deterioration.
items.mitigation_plan_description: First, the system must correctly identify at least 95 in every 100 eligible patients when tested against cases checked by an expert. The AI tool cannot go live unless it meets this accuracy threshold. The clinical safety team checks this before every release (DI-10BB41E9). Second, the system uses three different methods to search for relevant encounters: keyword search, full-text search, and meaning-based search. Using all three together reduces the chance of missing a patient. The technical team configures and maintains these search methods (DI-143F69EB). Third, each patient the system shortlists is given a ranked relevance score with supporting evidence from the notes. Clinicians can see why a patient was included or excluded. This is reviewed during clinical audit (DI-4746A178). Fourth, every episode is labelled as confirmed, excluded, or inconclusive. This makes it clear when the system is uncertain, so a clinician can review borderline cases. The clinical team reviews inconclusive cases as part of routine workflow (DI-37DDAADE). Fifth, the system must reach at least 85% accuracy when classifying episodes, measured against cases agreed by expert clinicians. The system cannot be deployed unless it meets this standard. The clinical safety team checks this at each release (DI-736B698B). Sixth, the rules the system uses to decide who is eligible are stored separately from the software code and are version-controlled. Changes to eligibility criteria can be made without a software release, and every change is recorded. The programme lead reviews and approves any changes (DI-1501326A). Seventh, any encounter the system fails to process is listed automatically, with the reason for failure shown. A member of the operations team can requeue failed encounters with a single action. The operations team reviews this list daily (DI-69CE20C1). Eighth, the AI workflow that classifies encounters uses managed rules, records its decision for each encounter, and must pass a test before any rule change takes effect. The technical team runs these tests before every update (DI-8CE01B3E). Ninth, any change to the system is risk-scored before it reaches live patients. High-risk changes are blocked from deployment until approved. The clinical safety officer reviews and approves high-risk changes (DI-7C5EC850). Tenth, all patient record data flows through a standard health data interface, and every audit result is exported through the same interface. This ensures data is not lost or corrupted in transit. The technical team monitors this continuously (DI-1795254D). Eleventh, the system processes each patient's full record within 10 seconds for 95 in every 100 patients. Slow processing is flagged automatically so delays do not cause patients to be missed. The technical team monitors processing times daily (DI-620FE631). The clinical safety committee reviews all these controls every quarter to confirm they are working as intended.

items.title: Quality check not run on some patient episodes
items.hazard: The system runs automatic quality checks on patient episodes to spot missing or incorrect information. If the quality check is not triggered for every type of episode, some episodes will not be checked at all.
items.hazardous_situation: A patient episode that contains missing or incorrect clinical information passes through the system without being flagged. The clinician reviewing the episode does not know a quality check was skipped. They may act on incomplete or wrong information.
items.harm: A clinician makes a clinical decision based on incomplete or incorrect information in a patient episode. This could lead to the wrong diagnosis, a missed diagnosis, or the wrong treatment being given. The patient could come to serious harm as a result.
items.mitigation_plan_description: Four controls reduce this risk. First, the quality check engine runs a configurable set of rules against every episode and records whether each episode passed or failed. It also stores a recommended action for any episode that fails. This runs automatically each time an episode is processed (DI-FC80B65A). Second, a live dashboard shows pass and fail rates for every rule, grouped by programme and organisation. It highlights trends so that a drop in coverage is spotted quickly. The clinical safety team reviews this dashboard regularly and can export the data for further checks (DI-E6A32FF5). Third, the system tells the reviewing clinician how each episode was classified, including whether a standard rule or a fallback method was used. This means the clinician knows if an episode was handled in an unexpected way (DI-8C236A1A). Fourth, when changes are made to an episode, the review screen shows a clear before-and-after comparison of every change. This helps the clinician spot anything that looks wrong before they approve it (DI-BC39B803). The clinical safety committee reviews audit data from the dashboard and incident reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

items.title: Spinal level labels mistaken for cancer staging codes
items.hazard: Spinal anatomy uses letter-number labels such as C3, T4, and L5 to describe vertebrae. Cancer staging also uses labels like T4 and N2 to describe tumour spread. The AI tool that reads notes cannot always tell these apart. When it sees 'T4' in a physiotherapy or back-pain note, it may treat it as a cancer staging code and save it to the patient record.
items.hazardous_situation: A GP writes a note about a patient's back or neck, for example 'C3-T4 facet areas' or 'NAGs C3'. The AI tool that reads notes picks out 'T4' as a separate item. The AI tool that decides if something is present, absent, or possible does not have a rule to check whether 'T4' is a spinal level or a cancer stage. It assigns a cancer staging clinical code and saves it to the patient record. The cancer audit system then picks up this code as if the patient has a confirmed cancer stage.
items.harm: The patient record now shows a cancer staging code that does not belong there. Cancer audit dashboards show the wrong stage distribution across the cancer pathway. Clinical quality teams may make incorrect improvement decisions based on this inaccurate data. Individual patients could also be incorrectly flagged as having a cancer stage, causing unnecessary concern or follow-up.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The AI workflow uses rules that constrain which clinical codes can be assigned based on the surrounding clinical context, reducing the chance that a spinal label is mapped to a cancer staging code (DI-3EA60D5A). This rule set is maintained by the clinical informatics team and reviewed whenever the AI workflow is updated. A separate gate checks and approves any change to the way staging surface forms are matched to clinical codes; changes must be reviewed, approved, and versioned before going live, and can be rolled back if a problem is found (DI-9FD54AD6). This gate is operated by the clinical safety team and runs for every proposed change. The AI tool that reads notes preserves the clinical context around each term, such as whether it appears in a musculoskeletal or oncology section, so that the correct clinical code can be chosen (DI-6A0B55A4). This is applied automatically during every note-reading process. The cohort builder applies rule-based checks across clinical codes, pathway stage, and patient details to catch records that do not fit expected patterns (DI-FE3FFE50). The clinical informatics team reviews cohort outputs at each audit cycle. The examples used to teach the AI are checked to ensure safety-critical entities such as cancer staging codes are represented accurately and in sufficient numbers, with a quality gate that blocks training if counts fall below a safe threshold (DI-AE477327). This check is run by the data science team before every training run. The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs, cohort outputs, and gate reports every quarter to confirm these controls are working as intended.

items.title: System fails to show the clinician the escalation threshold when reviewing a test result
items.hazard: The system holds guidelines that tell clinicians when a test result needs urgent action. If a guideline has not been linked to the correct test type, or the threshold value is missing, the system cannot show the warning. The clinician sees the result but gets no prompt that it has crossed a level requiring escalation.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician reviews an abnormal test result during a routine consultation. The system does not display the relevant guideline threshold because the link between the guideline and the test type is absent or incomplete. The clinician has no prompt to escalate and may assume the result is within acceptable limits.
items.harm: The clinician does not escalate the patient in time. A serious condition such as acute kidney injury or a dangerously abnormal blood count goes untreated or is treated too late. The patient suffers avoidable harm, which could include hospital admission, organ damage, or death.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The system shows the clinician the escalation threshold alongside every test result, with a comparison to similar patients on the same care programme. This runs automatically each time a result is reviewed (DI-49A8F570). The system is set up to suppress alerts only for results that are clearly within the normal range. Thresholds for suppression are agreed at programme level by the clinical team and reviewed regularly, so abnormal results always trigger a visible prompt (DI-79509E39). Every panel showing clinical information carries a permanent notice reminding the clinician that the output is a decision-support tool and does not replace clinical judgement. This notice is always visible and cannot be dismissed (DI-E609C4E5). When a clinician orders a test, the system displays the relevant guideline norms and comparator values at the point of ordering, reinforcing awareness of thresholds before results arrive (DI-F235845B). Partial results are shown to the clinician as soon as each step of the AI workflow is complete, rather than waiting for all steps to finish. This means the clinician sees available threshold information sooner (DI-CB07829F). All patient data coming into the system and all audit outputs leaving it follow a recognised clinical data standard, ensuring threshold records are structured consistently and can be checked for completeness (DI-1795254D). The system flags any test result where the displayed information diverges from the current guideline, and records a change history so the clinical team can spot patterns of missing thresholds. The impact review panel highlights these gaps for the clinical team to act on (DI-0C8FBAF7). The clinical safety committee reviews audit reports of threshold coverage and alert suppression settings every quarter to confirm all controls are working as intended.

items.title: The screen shows an out-of-date AI processing status to the clinician
items.hazard: The AI workflow stores a snapshot of its current status to speed up the screen display. If that snapshot is not refreshed after the AI finishes or changes state, the screen continues to show the old status. A clinician looking at the screen sees a status that no longer reflects what the AI is actually doing.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician checks the screen to confirm the AI has finished reviewing a patient's notes. The screen still shows the AI as running when it has already stopped, or as complete when it has failed. The clinician believes the AI result is ready and acts on incomplete or missing information without realising it.
items.harm: The clinician makes a clinical decision based on an AI result they believe is current and complete. In fact the AI did not finish correctly. The clinician may miss a diagnosis, overlook a medicine problem, or send a patient down the wrong care pathway. This could cause the patient serious harm.
items.mitigation_plan_description: A central status dashboard shows the live stage and next required action for the AI workflow. This gives every clinician and administrator a single, up-to-date view of what the AI is doing. The system updates this view automatically whenever the AI changes state (DI-BE09736F). A visible indicator appears on every administration page whenever the AI is actively learning from new examples. This means no one can miss that a learning process is under way and the results may not yet be final (DI-5E7E8CEF). When the AI classifies a patient encounter, any correction made by a reviewer is recorded immediately and linked back to the original information the AI read from the notes. This creates a permanent, tamper-proof record so the status shown always matches the most recent human review (DI-4F67189B). When a reviewer corrects an AI classification, that correction is fed back into the AI and recorded in the model registry. This means the displayed status reflects the latest agreed result, not an earlier automated one (DI-0ADE6A8E). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs of status mismatches every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

items.title: The system shows the wrong stage of a patient's care pathway
items.hazard: The AI tool that reads notes may calculate the wrong stage of a patient's care pathway. This can happen if the calculation contains an error or if the patient's record has not been updated recently. The system may then show a stage that does not match where the patient actually is in their care.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician sees an incorrect pathway stage on screen before or during a consultation. They do not realise the information is wrong. They make a clinical decision based on the incorrect stage, such as skipping a step that is still needed or repeating one that is already done.
items.harm: The patient receives the wrong care at the wrong time. For example, a needed test or treatment is delayed or missed entirely. This could cause the patient's condition to worsen, lead to a missed diagnosis, or result in a breach of waiting time targets with direct harm to the patient.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The system shows the clinician a confidence level alongside every AI-generated pathway stage. This tells the clinician how certain the AI is, so they can treat low-confidence information with extra care (DI-DA7584D8). The system generates a structured summary for each patient that includes the pathway stage and any safety alerts. The clinician reviews this before acting on pathway information (DI-30D9CC61). The system provides a clinic list view that shows pathway status and comparison information. The clinician can use this to spot stages that look out of place before the consultation begins (DI-CF03E4EA). The system generates a timeline of the patient's episodes and highlights any gaps in the pathway. This helps the clinician see if a stage appears to have been skipped or recorded incorrectly (DI-4885D9FF). The system calculates pathway intervals and automatically flags any breach of waiting time targets. This prompts the clinician to check the pathway stage is correct (DI-F3FD2B63). The system keeps patient data and clinical coding data in separate databases. This reduces the risk of a coding error corrupting the pathway stage calculation (DI-84F44836). The system provides AI-generated labels on pre-read summaries with direct links to the relevant guideline. The clinician can check the expected pathway stage against the guideline before acting (DI-6D2B03E0). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and reported incidents related to pathway stage accuracy every quarter to confirm these controls are working.

items.title: The tool does not show all the knock-on effects of a change to a clinical pathway
items.hazard: When a clinician reviews a proposed change to a clinical pathway, the tool may not show every downstream effect. For example, it may miss how the change affects related medicines, diagnoses, or referral steps. The clinician sees only part of the picture.
items.hazardous_situation: A clinician approves a pathway change without realising it will affect other parts of patient care. They do not know the full impact because the tool has not shown it. They act on incomplete information.
items.harm: Patients may receive the wrong treatment, miss a referral, or be given a medicine that no longer fits their pathway. Because the clinician did not see the full impact, the error may not be caught until the patient is harmed. The harm could be serious.
items.mitigation_plan_description: The tool shows a clear side-by-side view of what the pathway looked like before and after every proposed change. This helps the clinician spot differences quickly (DI-BC39B803). The tool also flags when a change does not match current NICE guidance, and highlights any history of similar changes that caused problems before (DI-0C8FBAF7). Before a clinician can approve any change, the tool requires them to complete a clinical impact assessment section. This step cannot be skipped (DI-59F2B21E). The tool checks whether the change affects any ICD-10 diagnosis codes or OPCS procedure codes and will not activate the change until this check is complete (DI-337D44DE). The tool tracks whether the change affects any NICE technology appraisals or quality standards, and sets time limits to make sure these are reviewed promptly (DI-44802DF3). If the data used to assess the impact is incomplete, the tool tells the clinician clearly before they make a decision (DI-88F20177). Every response from the AI includes a version identifier so the safety team can trace exactly which version of the AI produced the assessment (DI-0D26BE1B). The clinical safety committee reviews audit logs and near-miss reports every quarter to check that all these controls are working as intended.
